CLAUDE.md

Source: CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

What this is

zuroar gives R compressed sets of unsigned integers by wrapping CRoaring, the reference C implementation of Roaring bitmaps. A zuroar bitmap holds values from 0 to 2^32 - 1 and a zuroar64 bitmap values up to 2^64 - 1. Both answer membership, cardinality, rank, select and the set operations without materialising a vector, and serialise to the portable Roaring format that Java, Go, Rust, Python and C share. To R code a bitmap looks like a sorted vector without duplicates (x[i], head(), c()), and its API covers what pyroaring offers, in R form (design §5.1). It has no Imports and no LinkingTo; testthat and mirai are in Suggests. It is not a general set package, not a bit vector (no universe or [<-), not an algorithm library (every set operation is CRoaring’s) and, in v0.1.0, not a C API.

The specification is .agents/design.md, adopted from RFC 0061. It outranks this file: CLAUDE.md orients, the design doc decides. Its decisions D1 to D16 are the maintainer’s to overturn; open questions Q2 and Q5 are still open.

Current state

Scaffolded 2026-11-01 with create-pkg.sh (C, use_c()). Stages 0 to 4 merged on 2026-11-06: identity, vendored CRoaring, the zuroar class, its set algebra, and the switch from an external pointer to an ALTREP vector (design D17, re-planned the same day). The later stages, already written on the pointer in the stage-*-wip branches and pull request #19, rebase onto it. The roadmap in .agents/roadmap.md takes it to v0.1.0.

Stage tracking

Progress toward the next version is tracked as GitHub sub-issues, so the parent issue shows a progress bar such as “6 of 7”.

  • One parent issue per target version, titled with the bare version, for example v0.1.0. v0.1.0 issue: created by pkg-roadmap.
  • One sub-issue per roadmap stage, titled as the roadmap titles it, for example Stage 3 — R interface, and linking to that section. The number of stages is whatever the roadmap has; there is no fixed scale.
  • Every tracking issue carries the stage label, so it can be told apart from bug and feature issues and left out of open-issue counts.
  • Close a stage by merging its pull request. Put Closes #<n> in the body of the stage’s pull request. Never close a stage whose exit criteria are not met; record a deviation in the roadmap first.
  • The roadmap stays authoritative. The issues record which stages are done, not what a stage requires. Adding, removing or renaming a stage means editing the roadmap and the sub-issues in the same change.
  • Each stage has a CI tier, quick or full. The roadmap sets it, and quick is the default. See Continuous integration for what each means. The second-to-last stage, Full CI, runs the full set and fixes what it finds before v0.1.0 readiness.
  • Close the parent issue when CRAN accepts the version and it is tagged. Opening a parent issue implies at least one stage sub-issue; a parent with no sub-issues shows no progress on the board.

Versioning

A new package develops at 0.0.0.9000 and targets 0.1.0 for its first CRAN release. Set Version: 0.1.0 and the matching NEWS.md heading when the package enters Pre-flight. Bump to 0.1.0.9000 only after CRAN accepts it, never before: a .9000 version above an unreleased 0.1.0 heading is wrong.

Until the first release the R API may change freely. Sibling packages can still depend on this one before CRAN does, through Remotes: or LinkingTo:. None does yet. The design names zutable and zusearch, both proposed, as likely callers through Suggests; whether zutable would link to a zuroar header is open question Q2. A package that others wait on should reach CRAN first.

Commands

Run from the package root.

Rscript -e 'devtools::load_all()'                # compile src/ and load
Rscript -e 'devtools::document()'                # roxygen -> NAMESPACE, man/
Rscript -e 'devtools::test()'                    # full testthat suite
Rscript -e 'devtools::test(filter = "<name>")'   # one test file
Rscript -e 'devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE)'      # order independence
Rscript -e 'devtools::check()'                   # R CMD check
air format .                                     # format R sources

Architecture

Grows as stages land; see .agents/design.md §4.

  • src/croaring/: CRoaring’s roaring.c and roaring.h, upstream plus one patch. R compiles only top-level src/*.c, so nothing here builds on its own.
  • src/zro_roaring.h: the only way first-party C includes CRoaring. It sets NDEBUG, includes every system header CRoaring uses, defines printf as Rprintf while roaring.h is parsed, and hides CRoaring’s declarations.
  • src/zro_roaring.c: the wrapper unit, the only includer of roaring.c.
  • src/zro_init.c, src/zro_init.h: routine registration and the .Call prototypes.
  • src/zro_altrep.c: the representation (D17). A zuroar is an ALTREP double vector; its data1 is an external pointer, with a finaliser, to a zro_bitmap_t holding the CRoaring bitmap, its cached cardinality and a read cursor. zro_shell(), zro_attach() and zro_get() live here with the methods: Length, Elt, Get_region and Sum read through CRoaring; Dataptr refuses; Extract_subset builds x[i]; Duplicate is a copy-on-write copy; Serialized_state and Unserialize are the portable bytes. Three zro_test_* routines exist for the tests only.
  • src/zro_bitmap.c, src/zro_bitmap.h: the 32-bit bindings. Entry points allocate the result shell first (zro_shell()), then build the bitmap, then zro_attach() it, so no R allocation can leak one. zro_get() checks the class and zro_abort() signals a classed condition through the R-level zro_abort().
  • R/roar.R, R/methods.R, R/check.R, R/conditions.R: constructors, roar_add()/roar_remove()/roar_contains(), the vector methods, type checks (the C side checks each value), and the condition helper.
  • src/zro_algebra.c, R/algebra.R: Ops, c(), the named set operations, cardinality-only counts and shifting. Out-of-domain shifts are decided in R from min() and max() before CRoaring’s add_offset(), which drops silently.
  • src/zro_order.c, R/order.R, R/index.R: rank, select, next and previous, ranges, bounded extraction, storage, and positional access. [.zuroar turns the index into sorted runs of positions in R, and zro_subset() reads runs longer than 64 positions as a range intersection, shorter ones through an iterator. The ALTREP Extract_subset serves only C callers that bypass dispatch.
  • src/zro_portable.c, src/zro_portable.h: zro_portable_read(), the bounded reader (size check, safe deserialiser, validation), in plain C so tools/fuzz/harness.c fuzzes exactly what the package runs. Both roar_unserialize() and the ALTREP Unserialize (a readRDS()) use it.
  • src/zro_serial.c, R/serial.R: roar_serialize(), roar_unserialize() and roar_serial_config().
  • src/zro_info.c, R/info.R: zuroar_info().
  • src/zro_selftest.c: an unexported oracle hook, .Call(zro_selftest, x, y, optimize), so the build variants test CRoaring before the bindings exist.
  • R/zuroar-package.R carries @useDynLib zuroar, .registration = TRUE.

Invariants that are easy to break

These are fixed by the design before any code exists. Add each further one when a stage establishes it.

  • No R API inside a CRoaring call. Bindings validate R input, copy it into a uint32_t or uint64_t buffer, call CRoaring, then copy out. An R error raised in between would long-jump through CRoaring’s stack and leak or corrupt its state (design §4).
  • Untrusted bytes go only through the bounded path: roaring_bitmap_portable_deserialize_size(), then ..._deserialize_safe(), then roaring_bitmap_internal_validate(). The unsafe roaring_bitmap_portable_deserialize() is never called; it reads past the buffer on corrupt input (D8, §6.4).
  • Values stay exact. No silent NA and no inexact double: a value that does not fit the requested type is a zuroar_error_value (D2).
  • Every function returns a new bitmap and none modifies its argument; copy-on-write keeps that cheap (D4). An in-place shortcut changes a value another R variable still holds.
  • A zuroar is an ALTREP vector whose Dataptr never returns (D17, design §4, §14): it signals zuroar_error_unsupported, so no base or third-party C can expand the set, and Dataptr_or_null returns NULL. Its Serialized_state writes portable bytes and Unserialize reads them through the bounded path, so saveRDS() works. Consequences to keep in mind: identical(x, y) is that error (use ==), and so is expect_identical() on two bitmaps; Summary.zuroar calls the exact C sum itself, because R 4.6 was seen to skip the ALTREP Sum method and add in long double, a plain double on arm64 macOS; and tests call .Call() only through package functions (R/hooks.R), because rcnst compares uncompiled .Call() arguments with identical().
  • An attached bitmap is never modified. zro_attach() is the last write; every binding builds a new bitmap (D4). The read cursor in zro_bitmap_t holds a CRoaring iterator into the containers, and copy-on-write copies wrap containers without moving them, so the cursor stays valid for the bitmap’s life. An in-place CRoaring call on an attached bitmap would silently corrupt it.
  • ALTREP methods allocate nothing they do not protect, and call no R API while CRoaring runs. Get_region and Elt allocate nothing; Extract_subset, Duplicate and Unserialize follow the shell-then- attach order; Dataptr may signal (R’s own compact sequences do). A zuroar64 stays an external pointer, and every entry point checks it for null, which is what it becomes after readRDS(), erroring with zuroar_error_pointer naming roar_serialize() (D5). Skipping the check is a segfault.
  • R conventions at the boundary: ranges are inclusive and become CRoaring’s half-open [min, max); roar_select() counts from 1 where CRoaring counts from 0 (D6). Off-by-one errors here pass most tests.
  • No architecture flags in Makevars. No -mavx2 or -march; SIMD comes from CRoaring’s run-time dispatch (D3). CRAN rejects such flags.
  • CRoaring’s symbols stay hidden. The wrapper unit is the only includer of roaring.c and brackets it with #pragma GCC visibility push(hidden). Exported roaring_* names would clash with a sibling’s vendored copy in the same session.
  • Vector meaning never silently overrides set meaning. Where the two collide (rev(), [<-, x > 5, a shift out of the domain), the result is an error, not a conversion to a plain vector or a dropped value (D11, D12).
  • No Imports. A runtime dependency needs a design decision first.
  • CRoaring ignores the offset header when reading portable bytes; a corrupted offset reads the right set, not an error (design §8).
  • Comments must not name the unsafe deserialiser with parentheses. build-variants greps first-party src/ for roaring(64)?_bitmap_portable_deserialize( and fails on any match, comments included.
  • format(), print() and type_sum() never signal. R, testthat and rlang format objects while handling a condition; a second error there escapes the handler. For a zuroar64 they describe a null pointer instead, and the lazily registered pillar::type_sum() method keeps rlang’s backtraces from calling length() on one (design §6.6).
  • Allocate the shell before the bitmap. zro_shell(), then the CRoaring call, then zro_attach(). zro_abort() only when every bitmap is attached or freed.
  • Include CRoaring only through zro_roaring.h, and R headers after it. It must include each system header CRoaring uses before the hidden region. Under #pragma GCC visibility push(hidden), a libc declaration seen for the first time would be marked hidden too; GCC hides a re-declaration as well, which is why zro_roaring.h routes every posix_memalign declaration in the hidden regions to a static forwarder. The prelude must mirror roaring.h’s includes, under the same conditions or wider. Clang accepts what GCC rejects here, so a macOS build proves nothing. printf is undefined again after roaring.h, except in the wrapper unit; left defined, it rewrites the format(printf, ...) attributes in R’s headers.

Testing conventions

  • Self-sufficient. Every test builds its own inputs inside the test_that() block. No file-scope objects.
  • Self-contained. Global state goes through withr::local_*(), randomised input through withr::local_seed(). Tests write only under tempdir().
  • Assert on condition classes, never message text. Use expect_error(..., class = "<pkg>_<kind>_error"). Wording belongs in snapshot tests.
  • Order independence. devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE) is part of the definition of done.
  • Borrow a conformance suite before writing one. Mainstream implementations in Python, Java, Go or Node usually ship a test corpus. Use it as an oracle rather than inventing cases by hand. Here base R (union(), intersect(), setdiff(), %in%, findInterval()) is the oracle for every operation, and portable-format fixtures written by pyroaring and Java’s RoaringBitmap, with their generating scripts, are planned for Stage 5 (design §8).
  • Helpers live in tests/testthat/helper-*.R. helper-sets.R has gen_values(), sets that hit each container kind and the boundaries at 2^16, 2^31 and 2^32 - 1, and oracle(), which is sort(unique()). Call them inside test_that() after withr::local_seed().
  • length() is an integer when it fits. R’s dispatch converts a method’s double; compare with length(oracle(v)), not a double.
  • Interoperability fixtures in tests/testthat/fixtures/ are written by pyroaring 1.2.0 and Java RoaringBitmap 1.3.0 from sets.txt with tools/fixtures/make-fixtures (needs uv and a JDK); the fixtures workflow regenerates them and fails on any byte difference. Both writers produce identical bytes. pyroaring’s update() hangs on a stepped range; pass a list.
  • The mirai tests need the installed package (the daemon is a fresh R process), so they skip under devtools::test() and run under R CMD check. With a serial configuration they need mirai’s default dispatcher: dispatcher = FALSE does not apply it.
  • Keep the suite inside the CRAN time budget. It runs in seconds.

Definition of done

devtools::document() and devtools::check() clean, meaning 0 errors, 0 warnings and 0 notes. The one allowed note is “New submission” before the first release. devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE) green. CI green at the change’s tier: the quick profile for a quick roadmap stage or an ordinary pull request, the full profile for a full stage, Full CI, and every release. A user-facing change also needs a test, roxygen documentation and a NEWS.md entry.

Releasing to CRAN

  • CI is the pre-submission check. The pedrobtz/r-actions R CMD check runs --as-cran on the CRAN-like runners and containers, and it replaces win-builder, the macOS builder and R-hub. None of them is a release step, and cran-comments.md lists the CI legs as its test environments.
  • Entering Pre-flight. The roadmap’s feature stages are done, the version is set as in Versioning, NEWS.md and cran-comments.md are written, and CI is green. Only submission work remains.
  • Before submitting, run pkg-critical-review once the roadmap is implemented and fix what it files, then pkg-cran-review, and resolve every finding. Both skills are in pedrobtz/r-skills.
  • The pretest is automated and does not read cran-comments.md. A NOTE that is explained but not fixed gets the upload archived. Fix the NOTE, as under Vendored native code, instead of justifying it.
  • After acceptance, pkg-post-cran tags the submitted commit with the bare version, 0.1.0 (no v), publishes the GitHub release, bumps to 0.1.0.9000, closes the version’s parent issue and moves the board card.

Editing rules

  • roxygen comments are the source. Never edit man/ or NAMESPACE by hand.
  • Edit README.Rmd, not the generated README.md.
  • Keep prose simple and short. One idea per sentence.
  • Wrap roxygen text at 80 characters and run air format . on R sources.
  • Use lower_snake_case, and prefix internal native symbols with <pkg>_.
  • Keep hard runtime dependencies at zero unless a recorded design decision says otherwise.
  • Export and document public functions. Do not create roxygen topics for internal ones.

Continuous integration

Workflows come from pedrobtz/r-actions. Call those reusable workflows instead of writing bespoke ones, and pin a released tag rather than main. Pin a workflow that holds a write token, such as coverage.yml, to a commit, with the tag in a comment. The R-CMD-check workflow must call r-cmd-check.yml, because a hand-rolled one does not count as the pre-submission check. This package calls r-cmd-check.yml@v1; coverage.yml, vendor-upstream.yml and report.yml (write tokens) pinned to the v1 commit; fuzz.yaml (libFuzzer over zro_portable_read(), seeded by the fixtures) and fixtures.yaml (development only); native-checks.yaml (sanitizers, valgrind, LTO, rchk, analyzers, cran-special), gctorture.yaml and vendor.yaml at @v1. build-variants.yaml is the package’s own development-only job (design §7.4): it builds the default, no-AVX-512 and scalar variants, runs tools/check-symbols and the tests on each. pkgdown.yaml is the r-lib example workflow.

Small edits get a small run. The shared workflows look at the files a pull request changes, compared with its merge base:

  • Markdown only, such as README.md, NEWS.md or cran-comments.md, skips every check. Only coverage and the pkgdown site run.
  • DESCRIPTION or README.Rmd as well, and nothing else, adds one R CMD check on Ubuntu R-release.
  • Any other file runs everything.

So put a README or DESCRIPTION touch-up in its own pull request. Once a pull request changes code, every later push to it runs every workflow.

Quick by default, full by exception

The full profile is slow. gctorture at step 20 alone has taken 36 to 107 minutes on sibling packages. Waiting on it between roadmap stages was the main thing slowing roadmaps down, so:

  • Pull requests run the quick profile. It should finish in under five minutes. Here -fanalyzer (about 15 minutes over the amalgamation) runs on a pull request only with the full-ci label, and on every push to main (2026-11-06, Stage 3). Runner set-up (setup-r, apt) has taken 20 minutes on a bad day; that is the runner, not the profile. If it doesn’t, raise gctorture’s quick-step or trim quick-containers in the caller workflows; never cut the full profile.
  • A full roadmap stage takes the full-ci label and merges only on a green full run. The roadmap gives the reason in the stage’s **CI.** line, for example first compiled code, a PROTECT or finalizer change, a vendored library, or a Windows-only path.
  • Don’t wait on the full run a merge starts on the default branch, and cancel older full runs it supersedes. A failure that only the full set shows goes on the Full CI stage issue as a comment with the run link, and is fixed there. A failure the quick profile also shows is fixed now.
  • Full CI and v0.1.0 readiness wait for a green full run on their merge commit, and the release commit always needs one.
  • Locally, run gctorture(TRUE) on the code a C change touches when it is cheap; the full run is the authority.

Vendored native code

CRoaring 5.4.0 (tag v5.4.0, commit 20495fec4d1622b93284033a160f67d21a5aa8bb), the roaring.c and roaring.h amalgamation, used under the MIT side of its Apache-2.0/MIT dual licence (D9). Vendored in Stage 1.

  • Layout. src/croaring/ holds roaring.c, roaring.h, upstream LICENSE and AUTHORS. inst/COPYRIGHTS and the cph entry in DESCRIPTION declare it.
  • Pins. vendor.yaml (not src/vendor/PROVENANCE) records the tag, the commit, the SHA-256 of all four files, and the patch series, with the update procedure in its header comment.
  • The one patch. tools/patches/0001-remove-diagnostic-pragmas.patch deletes the six #pragma GCC diagnostic blocks, four in roaring.c and two in roaring.h. printf is handled by the macro in zro_roaring.h instead of a patch; tools/check-symbols proves no printf is linked.
  • Verification. tools/verify-vendor derives the tree from upstream plus the patches and compares it byte for byte. --canary must fail, and --write re-derives the tree for a bump. The vendor workflow runs it on every push and requires a change to src/croaring/ to change vendor.yaml too. vendor-upstream opens an issue weekly when CRoaring releases.
  • Symbols. tools/check-symbols runs after each build variant in the build-variants workflow. It fails on stdio, abort, exit or RNG references and on any exported CRoaring symbol.
  • tools/, vendor.yaml and the patches are build-ignored; the tarball ships only the patched result.

General rules for vendored code:

  • Pin a stable upstream release, never master or a release candidate.
  • Record the tag, the commit and the checksums, and write down the update procedure so the next bump is mechanical.
  • Keep upstream LICENSE and NOTICE beside the vendored code, declare the vendored code in DESCRIPTION and inst/COPYRIGHTS.
  • Keep the vendor tree clearly separated from first-party source, and record every local patch and why it exists.
  • CRAN’s compiled-code check applies to vendored code too. No stdout or stderr, no printf, abort, exit or system RNG may be linked, even behind a debug switch that never runs. Remove them with a patch in tools/patches/, list it in vendor.yaml, and make the vendor-verify script check “upstream plus exactly these patches”. Avoid diagnostic-suppressing pragmas too, because they draw their own NOTE. zuhtml is the reference: tools/patches/0002-no-stdio.patch and tools/verify-vendor. zuxml’s first upload was archived because it justified such a symbol instead of patching it.
  • Guard against regressions in CI: run nm -u on the built objects and fail on any of those symbols, so an upstream bump cannot bring them back.

Commits and pull requests

Short, imperative, sentence-case commit subjects, optionally scoped. Keep each commit focused and do not sweep in unrelated files. A pull request explains the user-visible outcome and the rationale, links related issues, lists the checks that were run and the tests that were skipped, and flags platform-sensitive or vendored changes. Performance claims need evidence.

Never commit or push to the default branch. Work on a branch, open a pull request, and leave it for review. Do not merge a pull request unless you are told to.

When you find a defect, in this package or in an upstream tool, open an issue for it rather than only working around it.

Working with skills

The portfolio’s workflow skills live in pedrobtz/r-skills (pkg-init, pkg-roadmap, pkg-implement, pkg-critical-review, pkg-cran-review, pkg-post-cran, pkg-readme); the general process skills are Superpowers. building-a-package.md in pedrobtz/packages walks through them in order. Both sets defer to this file where they overlap, so the settlements are recorded here.

  • One design. The specification is .agents/design.md, adopted from the package’s RFC in pedrobtz/packages/rfcs. A package with an adopted design is past brainstorming; a design change goes through the RFC, not a new spec. Superpowers’ default docs/superpowers/specs/ is not used.
  • Plans at two levels. .agents/roadmap.md holds the stages, one mergeable pull request each, with exit criteria and a CI tier (pkg-roadmap). Inside a stage, writing-plans breaks the work into tasks of one test cycle each, saved as .agents/plans/stage-<n>.md. The roadmap stays authoritative; a plan is scratch and is not kept in sync.
  • Build and merge. pkg-implement runs the stage loop: branch stage-<n>-<slug> from the stage issue, implement the plan with test-driven-development (Rscript -e 'devtools::test(filter = "<name>")' is the red/green command), open the pull request, merge on green at the stage’s CI tier. The confirmation the user gives at the start of that loop is the “told to merge” that Commits and pull requests requires, so the finishing-a-development-branch menu is not presented for stage pull requests. Any other pull request still waits for review.
  • Failures and claims. A failing check or test goes through systematic-debugging before a fix. “Green”, “done” and “ready for CRAN” are claimed only after verification-before-completion: run the command, read the output.
  • Review. requesting-code-review gates tasks inside a stage. pkg-critical-review reviews the whole package once the roadmap is implemented, with Posit’s reviewers, and files issues. CRAN’s reviewer email and GitHub review threads go through receiving-code-review.
  • Keep scratch out of the tarball. R CMD build reads .Rbuildignore, not .gitignore. It must list ^\.agents$, ^\.superpowers$ (the Superpowers task ledger), ^\.worktrees$ (if git worktrees are kept in the package directory; a sibling directory avoids the question), ^\.claude$, ^CLAUDE\.md$, ^AGENTS\.md$, ^CRAN-SUBMISSION$ and ^cran-comments\.md$. A stray top-level file is a NOTE, and the pretest archives on NOTEs.
